overview: “Khoisan” is an umbrella label for diverse Khoe and San peoples, not one kingdom or one established language family. The map’s vast outline and 4000 BCE to 1530 CE interval cannot define a single people’s territory or lifespan. The examples below identify particular communities and distinguish archaeological evidence from later recorded lives.

periods.title: Long regional histories
periods.summary: The early map interval sits within a much longer, diverse southern African archaeological past; named modern identities cannot simply be projected onto every site.

periods.title: Herding alongside other livelihoods
periods.summary: Sheep were present about two thousand years ago. Communities developed varied combinations of herding, gathering, hunting and exchange.

periods.title: Later voices enter written archives
periods.summary: Named speakers recorded stories and memories with Bleek and Lloyd, well after the map ends.

periods.title: A modern commemorative motto
periods.summary: South Africa introduced a national motto in /Xam.

items.text: Linguists distinguish Kx’a, Tuu and Khoe-Kwadi among the language families grouped under the southern African Khoisan label. Shared click sounds do not make them one language. Khoe-Kwadi itself includes communities with different histories of herding and gathering; a language name is not a job description.

A small toe bone from Spoegrivier Cave in Namaqualand helps date a major change. Researchers tested ancient proteins to distinguish sheep from similar wild animals, confirming a domestic sheep about two thousand years old. Herding arrived in a region where people already had deep knowledge of wild foods and animals.

An ostrich egg could become a water container. A Peabody Museum object collected in 1958 is catalogued as a possible San water carrier, perforated at one end. The Origins Centre describes plugged eggshell containers used to save scarce water: a remarkably practical use for something that began as an egg.

Food gathering also called for tools. The Origins Centre explains how San and Khoe women used pointed digging sticks to reach roots and bulbs, sometimes adding a stone weight with a hole through it. Its displayed example is dated 1970, documenting a later practice rather than fixing the invention’s date.

The same museum shows the engineering of a composite hunting arrow: connected sections and an attached tip that could separate after striking. Hunters also made adhesives to fasten components. These were carefully designed tools, requiring knowledge of materials, animal behavior and tracking.

Among Nama pastoralists in the Richtersveld, a house can travel with its owners. Domed homes use woven rush mats that can be taken apart when families move between grazing places. UNESCO’s account describes a living tradition: moving house can mean bringing the actual house along.

Richtersveld grazing is organized across communally managed land and seasonal stockposts. Pastoralists also gather useful and medicinal plants and preserve stories connected to places. Knowledge of when to move animals and where to find plants is part of caring for both a household and a landscape.

Tsodilo in Botswana preserves more than 4,500 rock paintings. Its hills and waterholes remain sacred to San and Hambukushu communities. The paintings span different periods and are not all securely dated; the site is a record of many visitors and inhabitants, not an illustrated diary of one timeless population.

sections.title: Named people, family memories and written words

items.text: The |Xam storyteller ||kabbo helped teach Wilhelm Bleek and Lucy Lloyd his language after being released from a Cape Town convict station. Their recordings from the 1870s and 1880s eventually supplied the 1911 book Specimens of Bushman folklore. Remembering the speakers’ names restores people to an archive often known mainly by its collectors.

A later childhood remembered in the archive belongs to |uma, who arrived in Cape Town in 1880 after abduction and separation from his family. He recalled his mother building their grass sleeping hut and gathering fruit and kernels. His affection for the fruit of the |kui tree preserves one child’s taste of home.

|uma, Da, Tamme and !nanni made hundreds of drawings and watercolors showing remembered plants, animals, foods and routes. At Mowbray they also built grass huts for play, including one for other children in the household. Their pictures preserve detailed environmental knowledge alongside the ordinary wish to play and remember home.

A modern written example of |Xam appears in South Africa’s coat of arms, introduced in 2000: “!ke e: /xarra //ke,” officially translated as “diverse people unite.” The special marks represent speech sounds. This is a modern commemorative use of the language, not a prehistoric inscription.

In 2017, South African San representatives set out their own research ethics code. It asks researchers to explain projects clearly, respect privacy, acknowledge knowledge and share benefits fairly. Communities were defining how outsiders should work with them, including protections for children and family life.

ending.text: The map stops in 1530, but these peoples’ histories do not. Later records document displacement and violence as well as family knowledge and creativity. Living Nama traditions and the San research code show communities maintaining culture and asserting rights in the present.
